newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Amsterdam sees busy October but no major rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Amsterdam sees busy October but no major rate rise.

text.p: The Dutch air cargo market is seeing a healthy start to October, and carriers are reluctant to increase rates despite the business pickup, a Reuter survey shows.

The jury remains out on whether business activity can be described as booming, while both carriers and forwarders seem extremely wary at becoming too enthusiastic over the market's prospects in case over capacity emerges again.
Although KLM has put out feelers for a possible increase in rates due to rising jet fuel prices, carriers are also generally unwilling to raise tariffs because of this situation.
However a KLM spokesman stressed that any increases are still only being considered.
There is a need in certain areas to increase rates, said Peter Schoute, chairman of the European Air Cargo Carriers Association and Cargolux country manager.
He added that the Dutch air cargo players are still reluctant to do so, but if KLM does raise tariffs, the rest may follow, he said but at present carriers seem to prefer 'to wait and see'.
Schoute also said that after mid-August, business showed a substantial increase as carriers flew full to destinations in the Middle East, Far East and to the U.S. west coast.
Many carriers are still optimistic that the last months of 1996 will make up for the first half, he added.
Those involved in the Netherlands-Asia Pacific cargo market are as usual, those that have the most reasons to be optimistic regarding the market. Rates too, are edging upwards in this market.

Perhaps the most significant shift upwards can be seen in the Hong Kong market. Rates have risen from a summer level of 2.45 guilders per kg to around 2.60 guilders per kg, with those on leading carriers as high as 3.10 guilders per kg.
The market also appears to be particularly healthy at the moment as the Hong Kong to Europe route has seen three rates increases in a short time.

Rates to Seoul have crept up from 3.60 guilders per kg to 3.65 guilders per kg and rates to Singapore have increased from 2.20 per kg to 2.25 guilders per kg and Narita has gone up by five Dutch cents to 4.20 guilders.
But carriers, despite increasing volumes and healthy rates, are not what could be described as "over the moon", although Amsterdam's air cargo market has more reason than most to be upbeat.

Schiphol showed a rise of 16.5 percent in August compared to last year. Airfreight volumes increased to 83,894 tonnes, an airport statement said, while between January and August there was an increase of 9.9 percent to 212,022 tonnes.
KLM saw a rise in August when it carried nine percent more airfreight despite the summer holiday season.

Sharp increases were especially evident in the Asian and Latin American markets, a KLM spokesman said. The company's South Asia/Middle East division saw a 30 percent increase and South and Central America saw volumes up by 20 percent, he said.
Cargo manager for Korean Airlines, Mike Zimmerman, said the carrier was keen to see the market retain its current capacity and rates levels.
He was reluctant to call for increases despite being hopeful that the carrier will maintain its volumes until the end of the year.

At the same time, he added, there is a fair amount of competition in the market from KLM and Asiana. His views were backed by other industry sources in that although business acitivity is in line with expectations, carriers seem to have learnt the hard way about the effects of too much capacity.
Zimmerman described the market as "fairly good but not booming".

Korean Airlines decided to put its brand-new Boeing 747-400 freighter on the Amsterdam-Seoul route, replacing a weekly B747- 200F. However, the planned introduction of a second freighter on this autumn on the Seoul-Amsterdam route has been postponed until spring 1997.

Achim van der Graaff, cargo manager for Cathay Pacific said business has seen a substantial pick-up in the last three or four weeks. He was optimistic that the last quarter of 1996 will be a busy one.
Cathay is probably not going to increase rates ex-Amsterdam although its subsidiary Air Hong Kong has lifted rates by around 10 percent on some routes, including those to Hong Kong, Dubai and Japan.
In general, the increases have been accepted by the market he said. At the same time, while carriers are not on the whole, implementing rises, they are edging up the rates for ad hoc shipments.
Imports to the Netherlands are 40 percent higher and exports are picking up, he added, with the possibility of the final quarter making up for the rest of 1996.

Van der Graff said one reason the carrier has seen a substantial pick-up may well be because it has recently changed its cargo handling system as Schiphol airport. Cargo imports now go directly to the consignee rather than through a handling agent, he added, which can sometimes save up to one or two days.

With an optimistic mood in the air, even those involved in the U.S. market are seeing an upturn. Schoute said the members of EACA had reported an increase in freight to the west coast and rates do seem to have firmed up, he added.
However, the U.S. east coast is not seeing such an improvement. There is still a lot of capacity going to the area and rates are under pressure, added Schoute.
Rates to the U.S. west coast have shown a marked increase from 1.80 guilders per kg to 1.90 per kg on Los Angeles but east coast levels reflect the situation there and have changed only slightly.

Jacques Heeremans, from general sales agent Inter Aviation Services, which represents all-cargo carrier, Polar Air said the airline has shown strong growth in imports from the Netherlands and a third weekly frequency looks likely.

Zygene managing director, J van der Woensel, whose company acts as gsa for Delta Airlines said growing demand was experienced in August and September, especially in the perishables market. There has been a stronger demand for Dutch vegetables and the the bulb season is now coming up, he added.

However, he said that the general cargo market is a little more slow to develop again after the summer season. The Netherlands-Middle East market maintains its reputation for being the most stable market.
Tijn Middendorp, Middle East director for MSAS, said the market was typical for the time of year and is busy. Dubai, especially seems particularly active, he said.

Middendorp tentatively suggests Dubai could be described as booming as freighters fly there fully booked. Rates have been too low in this market for some time, he added. But they too are showing signs of improvement.

Rates to Dubai can range anywhere from 1.40 guilders per kg to 1.65 guilders per kg but are usually on the higher end of this scale. Bahrain rates have seen an increase from 2.10 guilders per kg to 2.20 per kg.
Latin America is another stable market and one that was described by Dirk Hazenoot of Varig Brazilian Airlines as "stable and growing" but not "booming".
Though the market is in line with expectations, he said, rates are still under pressure and it looks like it will not be possible to increase them, he added.
However, rates have risen slightly on summer levels with Amsterdam-Sao Paolo at 5.30 guilders per kg from five guilders. Rates to Chile have increased to 5.55 guilders per kg from 5.5O per kg.

Van der Woensel, who also acts as gsa for LAN Chile, said that Brazil, Argentina and Chile are not booming but are growing considerably. Machinery and spare parts are major exports to Chile, he said as the Chilean government is putting a great deal of effort into backing industry.
Southern Africa has seen a slight ripple in the market as Dutch cargo and charter carrier, Martinair, starts its new South Africa service, but so far this has not had any major impact.
Meanwhile Cargolux's Schoute added carriers are not too worried about the new entrant as it is coming up to the peak perishables import season from South Africa, Kenya and Zimbabwe.

Rates have firmed up as the winter season starts, with South Africa increasing to 3.70 guilders from 3.65 guilders per kg to Johannesburg although the Nairobi rate has remained the same. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
